analysis.investment_thesis: Fedfina has delivered strong 3-year revenue CAGR of 32.2%, but the story is cracking — net profit actually fell from ₹245 Cr to ₹225 Cr in FY25 despite 30% revenue growth, signaling margin compression or rising credit costs. At a forward P/E of 11.35 there's a cheap-looking price, but I don't buy into a NBFC story where earnings are moving backwards while the loan book balloons.
key_strengths: Revenue growing at 32% CAGR (2022-25), reaching ₹1,973 Cr — the top-line growth narrative is intact
Forward P/E of 11.35 with a parent-bank backstop (Federal Bank, 60.79% promoter holding) limits downside
Diversified loan book across gold, SME, mortgage, and home equity reduces single-product concentration risk
key_risks: Profit DECLINED FY25: ₹245 Cr → ₹225 Cr despite 30% revenue growth — margin compression or rising NPAs are destroying the growth story
ROE of only 8.84% is well below my 12% threshold; a lending business failing to earn its cost of equity is a structural concern
Debt/Equity of 3.83 with negative OCF every year (0/4 positive) means this business depends entirely on capital markets — any credit tightening is existential
red_flags: EBITDA fell FY25 (₹415 Cr → ₹385 Cr) AND operating income fell (₹337 Cr → ₹316 Cr) — revenue growing 30% but profits shrinking is a major red flag
Negligible FII ownership at 0.66% — institutional money is voting with its feet
Operating CF negative all four years, Free CF deeply negative all four years — the business is a cash furnace
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Fedfina is an NBFC subsidiary of Federal Bank trying to grow its retail and SME loan book aggressively. On the surface the 3-year numbers look exciting — 32% revenue CAGR, 30% net profit CAGR — but FY25 completely breaks the story. Revenue jumped from ₹1,522 Cr to ₹1,973 Cr (+30%) yet net profit fell from ₹245 Cr to ₹225 Cr. That's the kind of divergence that tells me credit costs are rising fast or the company is pricing loans too aggressively to win share. When I see a financial company growing the loan book at 25%+ (assets went ₹11,138 Cr → ₹13,250 Cr) but earning only 8.84% ROE, I get nervous — they're putting a lot of capital to work for underwhelming returns.

The PEG picture is murky: using the forward P/E of 11.35 against even a modest 20% forward earnings growth gives a PEG of ~0.57, which looks cheap. But I don't trust that growth rate when FY25 showed actual earnings decline — Lynch's cardinal rule is to check whether the story is still intact before getting excited about low multiples. With negative free cash flow every year (inherent to lending, yes, but still ₹996 Cr negative in FY25), a D/E of 3.83, and virtually no FII interest, this is a "show me" stock. I'd want two consecutive quarters of improving NIM and ROE trending back above 12% before getting interested.
